read.sections.0.heading.source: New machines have changed work before
read.sections.0.heading.back: New machines have changed work before

read.sections.0.text.source: AI is not the first technology to change people's work. In England in the early 1800s, new machines in factories began to do work that skilled cloth workers had done by hand. Between 1811 and 1816, some of these workers, called Luddites, broke machines in protest. The machines were taking their work. Much later, from the 1970s, cash machines slowly spread to banks in the United States. Many people expected bank tellers, who handle money at the counter, to disappear. But a study from 2015 found that the number of tellers stayed about the same and even grew a little. Banks opened more branches, and tellers spent more time helping customers. That was one machine, long ago, so it can't tell us what AI will do.
read.sections.0.text.back: AI is not the first technology that changed human work. In England in the early 1800s, new machines in factories began to do work that was formerly done by hand by skilled cloth workers. Between 1811 and 1816, some of these workers, who were called Luddites, broke machines as a protest. The machines took their work. Much later, from the 1970s, ATM machines slowly spread to banks in the United States. Many people expected bank tellers, that is, workers who handle money at the counter, to disappear. But a study in 2015 found that the number of tellers stayed about the same, even rose a little. Banks opened more branches, and tellers spent more time helping customers. That was only one machine, in the past, so it cannot tell us what AI will do.
read.sections.0.text.note: "Cash machines" is "mesin ATM", the everyday Malaysian word. "Luddite" kept as the name.

read.sections.0.simpler.source: AI is not the first technology to change work. In the 1800s, new machines in England did the work of skilled cloth workers. Workers called Luddites broke some machines. From the 1970s, banks in the United States got cash machines. Many thought bank workers at the counter would disappear. A 2015 study found there were still about as many. Banks opened more branches, and workers helped customers more. That was long ago. It can't tell us what AI will do.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: AI is not the first technology that changed work. In the 1800s, new machines in England did the work of skilled cloth workers. Workers called Luddites broke some machines. From the 1970s, banks in the United States got ATM machines. Many people thought bank workers at the counter would disappear. A study in 2015 found their number was still about the same. Banks opened more branches. Workers helped customers more. That happened long ago. It cannot tell us what AI will do.

read.sections.1.text.source: Most jobs are made of many tasks. A new technology may automate some tasks, but not the whole job. When spreadsheets came to office computers in the United States, many bookkeepers lost their work. Yet the number of accountants grew. In 2025, the ILO, the United Nations agency for work, found that about one in four jobs in the world has some exposure to AI tools that write and make things. This means these tools could do some of the tasks in those jobs. It is not a count of jobs lost. Office jobs, such as clerks, have the most exposure. The ILO says most of these jobs are more likely to change than to disappear.
read.sections.1.text.back: Most jobs are made up of many tasks. A new technology may automate some tasks, but not the whole job. When electronic spreadsheets began to be used on office computers in the United States, many bookkeepers lost their work. However, the number of accountants grew. In 2025, the ILO, the United Nations agency for matters of work, found that about one in four jobs in the world has some degree of exposure to AI tools that write and produce things. This means these tools could do some of the tasks in those jobs. This is not a count of jobs lost. Office jobs, such as clerks, have the highest exposure. The ILO says that most of these jobs are more likely to change than to disappear.
read.sections.1.text.note: "Some exposure" is "sedikit sebanyak pendedahan" (exposure to some extent), so it is not read as "a little". "Pendedahan" for the ILO's "exposure" is a calque; a reviewer should check that learners will not read it as job loss.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: A job is made of many tasks. A new technology may automate some tasks, not the whole job. Spreadsheets did sums for office workers. Some people who added up numbers lost their work. But there were more accountants. In 2025, a United Nations group studied AI that writes and makes things. About one in four jobs has some exposure to it. It could do some of their tasks. This is not a count of lost jobs. Office jobs have the most exposure. Most will likely change, not disappear.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: One job is made up of many tasks. A new technology may automate some tasks, not the whole job. Electronic spreadsheets did calculations for office workers. Some people whose work was adding up numbers lost their work. But the number of accountants grew. In 2025, a United Nations group studied AI that writes and produces things. About one in four jobs has some exposure to it. That AI could do some of their tasks. This is not a count of jobs lost. Office jobs have the most exposure. Most of them will probably change, not disappear.

read.sections.2.heading.source: Some people gain, and some people lose

read.sections.2.text.source: Change at work is often uneven. In 2024, the International Monetary Fund warned that AI could help some workers do more, and take important tasks from others. It also said AI will probably make inequality worse unless governments act. In Millbrook, the water office works faster. Two clerks moved to the help desk after training, but one lost her work. Training and fair rules can help. Workers, employers and governments can decide together how new tools are used.
read.sections.2.text.back: Change at the workplace is often uneven. In 2024, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) warned that AI could help some workers do more work, and take important tasks from other workers. The IMF also said that AI will probably make inequality worse unless governments act. In Millbrook, the water office now works faster. Two clerks moved to the help counter after training, but one clerk lost her work. Training and fair rules can help. Workers, employers and governments can decide together how new tools are used.

read.sections.2.simpler.source: In 2024, money experts said AI may help some workers. It may take big tasks from others. It may make inequality worse, unless leaders act. After training, two Millbrook clerks moved to the help desk. One lost her work. Training and fair rules can help. Workers and leaders can decide together how to use AI.
read.sections.2.simpler.back: In 2024, finance experts said AI may help some workers. AI may take important tasks from other workers. AI may make inequality worse, unless leaders act. After training, two Millbrook clerks moved to the help counter. One lost her work. Training and fair rules can help. Workers and leaders can decide together how to use AI.
read.sections.2.simpler.note: "Money experts" is "pakar kewangan" (finance experts); "big tasks" is "tugas penting" (important tasks), as in the standard text.

write.example.source: I chose the clerks at the Millbrook water office. AI changed their work because a new tool now reads most forms. The office gained, because the work is faster. Ines gained too, because after training she moved to the help desk. The third clerk lost out, because she has no work there now. This is like the cloth workers in the 1800s. One thing that would make it fairer is training for every clerk, so nobody is left without work.

watch.summary.source: This video asks if machines and AI will take away people's jobs. People have worried about this many times before. In the United States, machines replaced many workers in the 1920s and 1930s. It happened again around 1960. Machines took work on farms, in factories and on telephone lines. But most people still found work. Technology makes some new jobs, such as building and fixing machines. It also makes things cheaper. Then people spend money on other things, like haircuts or eating out, and those need workers too. Some experts say AI is different, because it can do many kinds of work. The video says the bigger question may be who gains. The gains from technology have not been shared fairly. The rules people choose can change that.
watch.summary.back: This video asks whether machines and AI will take people's jobs. People have worried about this many times before. In the United States, machines replaced many workers in the 1920s and 1930s. This happened again around 1960. Machines took work on farms, in factories and on telephone lines. But most people still found work. Technology creates some new jobs, such as building and repairing machines. Technology also makes goods cheaper. Then people spend money on other things, like haircuts or eating out, and all those need workers too. Some experts say AI is different, because AI can do many kinds of work. This video says the bigger question may be who profits. The gains from technology have not been shared fairly. The rules people choose can change that.

educatorNotes.0.source: One exposure figure in learner text, on purpose. The ILO's (May 2025, with Poland's NASK) is potential exposure to generative AI: 25% of the world's jobs are in occupations where these tools could do some tasks. It is not a count of jobs lost, and the ILO expects most to be transformed rather than replaced; clerical jobs are the most exposed, and in rich countries the jobs most at risk of automation are 9.6% of women's jobs against 3.5% of men's. The IMF's figure (January 2024) has a wider scope: almost 40% of the world's jobs, and about 60% in advanced economies, are exposed to AI in general, with roughly half of those likely to gain and half to see lower demand. Learner text keeps only the IMF's warning about inequality, without its numbers, so the two estimates aren't mixed up. The bank teller example is US data from the 1970s to the 2000s (James Bessen, 2015); it shows one past case, not a forecast for AI. The spreadsheet example is from NPR (2015).
educatorNotes.0.back: One exposure figure in learner text, on purpose. The ILO's figure (May 2025, with Poland's NASK) is potential exposure to generative AI: 25% of the world's jobs are in kinds of jobs where some tasks could be done by these tools. It is not a count of jobs lost, and the ILO expects most to change, not be replaced; clerical jobs are the most exposed, and in rich countries the jobs most at risk of being automated are 9.6% of women's jobs against 3.5% of men's jobs. The IMF's figure (January 2024) is wider in scope: almost 40% of the world's jobs, and about 60% in advanced economies, are exposed to AI in general, with roughly half of them likely to benefit and the other half likely to be less needed. Learner text keeps only the IMF's warning about inequality, without its numbers, so that the two estimates are not mixed up.
